## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals
## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [Record](#11-record) describes.

## 8. Review
## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it,
without the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else
runs on it. `GOALS.md` is the exception: a change to it is proposed, never made, since it
is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption
# A side campaign's first plan: what landed before a schedule, and how far its decomposition reaches

Status: `open`. Filed by glibc-crustify `planner/run-1` (2026-11-13), under the default
`repair` autonomy (`crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` gives no `evolution` answer): an improvement,
proposed rather than made.

## Signal

Rules a run had to work out by hand that the skills should state (`evolution` §2, "a rule
an agent works around"). glibc-crustify's first planner run met a repository with no plan, whose
`struct tm` (`b7d01b0`, `ea38101`, `8220840`) and `__errno_location` (`787a802`) wrappers
had landed on `crustify/devel` with no `schedule.json`, no wave and no batch. It was asked
to record them as landed rather than schedule them again, and to plan three more entities
(`_IO_FILE`, `fprintf`, `stderr`), without a wavefront database over the system's glibc.

1. **Landings with no schedule.** `schedule-schema` gives a started wave's record only to
   waves whose batches ran (§2, §4, §5), and `scheduling` drops an item a batch has landed
   (§3). Nothing says how a plan records an item that landed before any schedule existed,
   so a planner either schedules it again or leaves it out of the order entirely. The run
   recorded each as a `done` wave of its module, with one `done` `wrap` batch whose
   `commits` are the commits that touched its home, in landing order, and numbered them
   before the `todo` waves (`crustify/artifacts/schedule.json`, waves 0 and 1). Those are
   progress fields, the assistant's, which the run wrote because its task message asked.
2. **How far a side campaign's decomposition reaches.** `decomposition` §2 covers "the
   selected target and its complete imported producer closure: every translation unit the
   build compiles in scope". For a side campaign over a system library, whose scope is a
   few entities and which is wrapped, never built or ported, a body-deep closure would pull
   in most of the library (`stdio-common/fprintf.c` calls `__vfprintf_internal`, which
   reaches locales, wide characters and the allocator). The wavefront skill schedules a wrap
   campaign in API mode, but counts the modules' dependency records "from a schedule of the
   whole closure" (Decomposition › Dependencies) without saying in which mode. The run
   decomposed only the TUs that own a scoped entity and what their public signatures reach
   (`libio/genops.c`, the owner of `_IO_FILE`), and counted the dependency records over
   that signature graph.

## Destination

The spec: `schedule-schema` §5 (Re-planning) and `scheduling` §3 for (1); `decomposition`
§2 and the wavefront skill's Decomposition › Dependencies for (2).

## Binding and porting

### Binding › Safe boundary

Before a batch lands, a scan with `--sites fn.unsafe.pub raw_ptr.field.pub
raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub` lists the public
`unsafe fn`s and the raw pointers on the safe public interface, and each of those sites
that belongs to the batch's changeset and that a safe variant could replace is fixed.
Its `--sites` also name the unsafe code outside both regions,
`code.unsafe_block.of_which.outside_regions`, another crate's macro expansions included,
which the `unsafe_code` lint misses, and `fn.unsafe.of_which.outside_regions.pub` and
`.priv`: outside the raw bindings, each of those sites in the batch's changeset is moved
into its region.

## Accounting

### Accounting › Landing cells

A batch's row in the dashboard's `Batches: safety audit` table is the change in each of
the Safety audit's metrics, from a scan of the tip its landing rebased onto to a scan of
the tree it lands.

### Accounting › API stability

`ffimap api` measures a safe crate's consumer-facing API per C item, from rustdoc JSON, as
its `docs/api.md` describes, read in full before its first use. A C item is the
`<kind>::<path>` of a `Wraps` or `Replaces` anchor, its surface every stand-in the anchor
names and the handles and owners tied to it, each judged by the contract
[`binding-types`](../../rust/binding/types/SKILL.md)' Safe layout section gives a consumer:
the methods every form offers, its reborrows and dereferences, and the traits a consumer
can use, never a form's raw access or seams. A batch generates the safe crate's rustdoc
JSON on the tip its landing rebased onto and on the tree it lands, with a nightly whose
`format_version` the tool supports, and ffibox's, with private items, for the contracts of
the forms it defines:

```bash
cargo +<nightly> rustdoc -p <crate> --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json
ffimap api diff <base>.json <tree>.json --dep <ffibox>.json --items "<the worklist's keys>" --format json
```

Each item comes out `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed` or `new`, with its anchor's
move from `Wraps` to `Replaces` where a port made it. The batch's row in the dashboard's
`Batches: API stability` table counts them over its worklist, and over the crate's
unattributed public items, compared per module.

### Accounting › Records

An unseeded scan of the unsafe and FFI surface is recorded at each batch's, wave's and
the campaign's end, as `ffimap.json` in its artifact directory: a batch's in the run dir
of the run that landed it, a wave's in its wave's dir, as `layout` spells it, and the
campaign's in `crustify/artifacts/`. A module's end is the scan of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items.

---
name: ffimap
description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), before planning an audit's worksets, and when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB."
---

# ffimap

ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.

It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```

Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \
    --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \
    > <file>.json
```

In a port campaign, a scan names with `--features` the export feature of every module not
yet switched, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Export features section
names them, so that the `ffi_export` gateways compiled under them are counted. Every scan
names the module's unsafe regions, as the conventions' Unsafe regions section names them,
with `--regions`.

Two scans are compared only when they name the same seams, regions and features.

Its counters form one tree, each named by its dotted path into the scan's `counts`, as
ffimap's `docs/schema.md` describes; a metric is a counter, or a combination of counters
that schema allows: a partition's leaves summed, a share read against the record it cuts,
or subtracted from it. `--sites <counter> ...` also lists where each named counter's
increments are, and takes leaves only, such as `fn.unsafe.pub`; the workspace is named
before it. The counters that recur:

- `fn.unsafe.pub`, the public `unsafe fn`s, the crate's public unsafe surface, of which
  `fn.unsafe.of_which.other.pub` are those neither a trait nor a seam required; and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, the raw pointers in
  their signatures;
- `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`, the
  raw pointers in public fields and in the signatures of public safe fns, together
  `raw_ptr.total.safe.pub`, the raw pointers on the safe public interface; and their
  `of_which.void` shares, the type-erased ones among them;
- `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, the references to a cell, less their
  `of_which.self_in_ref_accessor` and `of_which.self_in_trait_impl` shares, the positions
  ffibox sanctions: references to C memory where a handle belongs, which assert `noalias`,
  `readonly` or validity over memory C may write; `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std`, the same
  of the raw C structs; and `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`, the borrows,
  slices and strings formed from a raw pointer, over bytes C must neither free nor change
  while they live;
- `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`,
  each an unchecked assertion that a value may move to or be shared with another thread;
- `raw_ptr.deref.wr` and `raw_ptr.deref.rd`, raw-pointer writes and reads, each a pointer
  the implementer vouches is non-null, aligned, live, initialized and unaliased by a live
  reference; and
- `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}` and
  `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`, the types that hold a raw pointer and
  tear it down or copy it by hand, and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none.{pub,priv}`, those
  that declare nothing about it. Each of these five also has a `.total`, the sum of its two
  leaves, which is no leaf for `--sites`.

ffimap is neither complete nor sound: its sites are where review starts, not all it
covers. It does not count the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, such as a reference
or lifetime-annotated handle made from a raw pointer by `&*p`, `from_ptr`, `from_raw` or
`from_raw_parts`, or changed by a `transmute`: those are found in the source.

What follows is how ffimap serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffimap adds there.

/opt/venv/bin/ffimap

usage: ffimap [-h] [--sites COUNTER [COUNTER ...]]
              [--sys-crates CRATE[,CRATE...]] [--seams NAMES]
              [--regions NAMES] [--barriers NAMES]
              [--features FEATURE[,FEATURE...]] [--ffibox]
              WORKSPACE

Scan a Rust crate's unsafe surface and raw-pointer usage with a rustc driver
over HIR and typeck. Reproducible: same tree, same bytes. Needs the crate to
compile; when it does not, there are no counts rather than approximate ones.
It says HOW MUCH unsafety is there, never which of it is wrong.

positional arguments:
  WORKSPACE             Directory of the Cargo workspace (or package) to scan.

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --sites COUNTER [COUNTER ...]
                        Also report where these counters' increments are in
                        the source: a `sites` record beside `counts` with one
                        list per counter. Takes a counter's dotted path down
                        to its LEAF (e.g. raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub,
                        ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.pub,
                        code.unsafe_call.ffi): a path that stops at an arm
                        above one validates and then reads empty, since the
                        driver emits by leaf. Line totals have no sites.
  --sys-crates CRATE[,CRATE...]
                        Crates whose #[repr(C)] types are C's: the crate's own
                        bindings and any other crate it reaches C through,
                        such as `libc`. The field walk descends through them
                        too, so a pointer a scanned type holds through one is
                        counted as the scanned crate's to manage. Nothing is
                        discovered: a Cargo `links` key and a `*-sys` name
                        both over-report, so unnamed means the peel set is the
                        scanned crate alone.
  --seams NAMES         Function names that are seams -- the conversion
                        between a wrapper and its raw pointer (`raw`,
                        `from_raw`, `as_ptr`, `from_ptr`). Newline- or comma-
                        separated, so `--seams "$(cat seams.txt)"` works. They
                        are counted as usual and ALSO reported as the
                        `of_which.seam` share of each fn-signature counter, so
                        a reader can tell plumbing from the pointer management
                        a consumer of the safe API actually faces. ffimap
                        never guesses the names.
  --regions NAMES       Module names that are regions -- the modules a crate
                        confines a kind of code to, such as its unsafe FFI
                        (`ffi_import`, `ffi_export`). Newline- or comma-
                        separated. The unsafe blocks are then reported by the
                        region they sit in, as
                        code.unsafe_block.of_which.region.<name>, with the
                        rest as outside_regions, and the unsafe fns outside
                        every region as fn.unsafe.of_which.outside_regions. A
                        module is in a region when it, or a module enclosing
                        it, has one of these names. ffimap never guesses the
                        names.
  --barriers NAMES      Function names that are the crate's own panic
                        barriers: helpers that call `catch_unwind` for their
                        caller, such as a `wrap(|| ...)`. Newline- or comma-
                        separated. A fn with a foreign ABI that calls one
                        counts in fn.extern_abi.of_which.catches_unwind, as
                        one calling `catch_unwind` itself does. ffimap never

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""end-gates: run a wave's or a module's end gates over a snapshot of a tree.

    end-gates <tree> --logs <dir> [--stages plain,asan-ubsan,tsan,miri,bsan]
              [--rev <rev> | --working-tree] [--package <name>] [--runner <cmd>]
              [--link <path>]... [--skip-file <file>] [--stage-env <stage>:<K>=<V>]...
              [--timeout <seconds>] [--parallel <n>] [--nightly <toolchain>]

The gates of testing-gates' Regressions section, run exactly so:

1. The tree's commit (`--rev`, HEAD by default), or its working tree with
   `--working-tree`, is copied to a snapshot, `<tree>/crustify/tmp/gates-<label>`, so that
   work goes on in the tree while the gates run. Each submodule, and each `--link` path
   (such as the variants' builds dir), is symlinked from the tree into it, and the snapshot
   is made a git repository, since a test may discover the repository it runs in.
2. Each skip of `--skip-file` is checked against its test binary's `--list` before any
   stage runs: a skip that names no test, or that would also skip another, since libtest
   skips by substring, fails the run.
3. The stages run in the order given:
   - a variant (`plain` and each sanitizer but `bsan`): the workspace's tests,
     `<runner> <variant> test --workspace --no-fail-fast`, with that stage's skips;
   - `miri`: the package's test binaries built once on the pinned nightly, then one
     `cargo miri test` per test binary, side by side, each skipping `compile_fail`;
   - `bsan`: the test binaries built once, then one invocation per test binary, side by
     side, each under `--timeout`, with that stage's skips.
4. Each run writes `<logs>/<stage>[-<binary>].log`; `<logs>/summary.json` and
   `summary.txt` record each run's command, exit status, duration, test-result lines and
   failed tests. A run that exceeds its timeout reports `timed_out`.

The skip file holds one skip per line, `<stage> <binary> <exact test name>`, the binary
being `lib` or an integration test's name; `#` starts a comment. A variant stage's skips
apply to every binary of the workspace.

The job count is the environment's: `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS` for builds, `RUST_TEST_THREADS` for
each binary's tests, as concurrency describes. The exit status is 0 when every run
passed, 1 when any failed, and 2 when the run could not start.

Standard library only.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import shlex
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

PER_BINARY = {"miri", "bsan"}


class Refused(Exception):
    """The run cannot start: a bad argument, tree or skip."""


def git(tree: Path, *args: str) -> str:
    return subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(tree), *args], check=True,
                          capture_output=True, text=True).stdout


def snapshot(tree: Path, dest: Path, rev: str | None, links: list[str]) -> None:
    """Copy `rev`, or the working tree when it is None, to `dest`, a fresh git repository."""
    if dest.exists():
        shutil.rmtree(dest)
    dest.mkdir(parents=True)
    if rev is not None:
        with subprocess.Popen(["git", "-C", str(tree), "archive", rev],
                              stdout=subprocess.PIPE) as archive:
            subprocess.run(["tar", "-x", "-C", str(dest)], stdin=archive.stdout, check=True)
        if archive.returncode != 0:
            raise Refused(f"git archive {rev} failed")
    else:
        files = git(tree, "ls-files", "-co", "--exclude-standard", "-z")
        names = [f for f in files.split("\0") if f and (tree / f).exists()
                 and not (tree / f).is_dir()]
        packed = subprocess.run(["tar", "-c", "-C", str(tree), "--null", "-T", "-", "-f", "-"],
#!/bin/bash
# Run cargo against one crustify prebuild of libgit2, instrumenting Rust to match.
#
#   crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]
#
# <variant> is a `variants` key of crustify/artifacts/build.json: plain, coverage, asan-ubsan,
# tsan or bsan. Each variant uses its own target dir under target/.
# The safe crate's build script, in campaign mode, links the variant's static archive (its
# `static` in build.json) into each test binary, so the C runs under the instrumentation the
# Rust is built with here, one runtime serving both. Set CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR to a private build
# of the variant, which carries the same archive, to link it instead of the shared one.
set -euo pipefail
variant=${1:?usage: cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]}
shift
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$here/target/$variant}
# pcre2-sys links the variant's side-campaign PCRE2, the one libgit2's C links, rather than
# building its vendored copy, which would shadow it in every test binary. The side campaigns'
# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done
case $variant in
  plain)
    exec cargo "$@" ;;
  coverage)
    # Source-based coverage on the pinned nightly, against the variant's clang-instrumented C,
    # which each test binary links statically, so that rustc's profiler runtime counts both;
    # crustify/scripts/coverage/ measures the suites as the testing spec's Coverage section does.
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/profraw/%p-%m.profraw}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  asan-ubsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address"
    export ASAN_OPTIONS=${ASAN_OPTIONS:-detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1}
    export UBSAN_OPTIONS=${UBSAN_OPTIONS:-print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  tsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    # glibc's tzset locks what TSan cannot see: see tsan.supp.
    export TSAN_OPTIONS=${TSAN_OPTIONS:-halt_on_error=1:suppressions=$here/crustify/scripts/tsan.supp}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" -Zbuild-std --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  bsan)
    # trybuild's nested cargo build does not finish under BorrowSanitizer, and the
    # compile-fail suite is a compile-time check the plain variant already runs.
    # Under parallel test threads BorrowSanitizer's GC can take longer than its default
    # 10 s hang threshold to bring every thread to a safepoint, and then aborts; give it
    # 120 s rather than serialize the tests.
    export BSAN_OPTIONS=${BSAN_OPTIONS:-gc_hang_threshold_ms=120000}
    if [ "${1:-}" = test ]; then
      case " $* " in
        *" -- "*) exec cargo bsan "$@" --skip compile_fail ;;
        *) exec cargo bsan "$@" -- --skip compile_fail ;;
      esac
    fi
    exec cargo bsan "$@" ;;
  *)
    echo "unknown variant: $variant" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
# TSan suppressions for the campaign's tsan variant (crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh).
#
# glibc's tzset (reached through mktime/localtime from git_signature_now, on every reflog
# write) updates its timezone state under an internal __libc_lock that ThreadSanitizer
# cannot see, glibc not being instrumented: two threads writing reflogs are reported as a
# race on the strings tzset_internal frees and strdups. The state is lock-protected.
race:tzset_internal

content.content:
## 3. Building a report

A report is leaves divided and subtracted, named by their paths. Three rules
make the arithmetic sound:

- a partition may be summed, an `of_which` may not, and an `as` never with the
  types above it. Two shares of one record overlap, so
  `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop + impl_clone` is not a quantity, while
  `pub + priv` is the record;
- a rate stays inside one record, or between a record and the denominator
  emitted for it: `fn.unsafe.pub / fn.total.pub`, `code.loc.unsafe /
  code.loc.total`, `ty.storing_raw_ptr.pub / ty.total.pub`. Dividing across
  prefixes mixes grains -- signature positions by lines of code says nothing;
- a share is read against the record it cuts, and the remainder is a
  subtraction: `wrapper.as.borrowed.std.pub` less its two sanctioned shares is
  the convention's unsanctioned surface.

### 3.1 The readings worth taking

Each reading below names the leaves it is made of. The figures are not here: a
reading of one crate is in [`analysis.md`](analysis.md), where it is the
evidence for a rule, and a reading of several is in
[`examples/README.md`](../examples/README.md), where three real documents are
tabulated side by side. A figure copied into this document would be a second
copy to keep current, and the counters are what this document is for.

**How much of the bindings has a cell.** Under `--ffibox` with the `-sys`
crates named, `ty.ffibox.sys.of_which.raw_ptr_in_sys.of_which.wrapped` against
`raw_ptr_in_sys` is the share of the C types the bindings hand around by pointer
that the crate has given a cell, and `used` against it the share the crate
touches at all, so the gap between the two shares is the C it touches
without a cell ([ffibox.md](ffibox.md#8-where-the-declarations-mention-a-cell)). Against `ty.ffibox.sys.total` it reads low by
construction, since a by-value struct needs no cell.

**How much of the C functions has a wrapper.** Under `--ffibox` with the
`-sys` crates named, `fn.ffibox.wrapper.of_which.unique` against
`fn.ffibox.sys.total` is the share of the C functions the bindings declare
that the crate annotates a wrapper for, and `fn.ffibox.sys.of_which.used`
against it the share it calls at all. The annotation is the only record of
what a wrapper wraps, so an unannotated wrapper reads as none; the alias is
the one the Crustify conventions require. `fn.ffibox.wrapper.total` against
`unique` is how many variants a wrapped function was forked into on average.

**Which `unsafe fn`s nothing required.** `fn.unsafe.of_which.other` is the
unsafe surface the crate chose: no trait declared the method unsafe and no
seam adopts a pointer through it. Read it against `fn.unsafe`, and its `pub`
leaf against `fn.unsafe.pub`, rather than subtracting `in_trait_impl` and
`seam`, which overlap.

**What a consumer meets without writing `unsafe`.**
`raw_ptr.total.safe.pub` is the raw pointers on the safe public interface,
`fn.unsafe.pub` against `fn.total.pub` the public unsafe surface, and
`raw_ptr.field.pub` the pointers a public field hands over with no `unsafe` at
all.

**How much unsafe, and where it sits.** `code.loc.unsafe / code.loc.total` is
the density and `code.unsafe_block.total` the number of blocks; read both,
since folding small blocks into large ones moves one and not the other.
`code.unsafe_block.of_which.ffi_export` subtracts the gateways a port campaign
generated, and the `code.unsafe_call` arms say what the unsafe is for: `ffi`
is the boundary, `rust` is the standard library's constructors and the crate's
own helpers, `intrinsic` is `transmute` and its siblings.

**What the crate wrote, as opposed to what a macro did.** Subtract
`fn.total.of_which.macro` from `fn.total`, and
`ty.impl_trait.of_which.derived` from `ty.impl_trait`. A comparison of two
crates without those shares is partly a comparison of how much boilerplate
each spells.

**What the crate declares about the pointers it manages.**
`ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none` against `ty.storing_raw_ptr` is the types
that hold a pointer and say nothing about it. The other shares say what the
rest declared -- `impl_drop`, `impl_clone`, `ffibox` -- and `pub_field` is the
opposite of a declaration.

**Whether a convention is kept.** Under `--ffibox`,
`ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std` less `self_in_ref_accessor` and
`self_in_trait_impl` is the bare `&Foo` surface the convention says should be a
handle. `as.owned.std` and `as.by_val` against `as.owned.ffibox` say how much
of a cell's storage the crate holds itself rather than through ffibox's
owners. `ty.ffibox.wrapper.of_which.no_seam_trait` is the cells a generic
handle has to special-case, and `fn.sig.of_which.ffibox` whether the
vocabulary reaches the interface at all.

**What the trait impls do.** `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std`'s arms say which of
the crate's adopted traits act on what it wraps: `drop` and `clone` run its
lifecycle, `send` and `sync` are claims about threads, `ref_forming` can hand
out a reference to it. Under `--ffibox`, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.ffibox`'s
`layout` and `policy` say how much of the convention is the cells' layout and
how much their lifecycle.

**Whose shape the pointers in trait impls are.** `fn_sig_trait_impl` is read
through its `of_which` arms, never bare: one crate's are a convention's
lifecycle strategies, another's its own private helpers, a third's one local
conversion trait, and the bare figure is the same for all three.

**The test code, beside the library and never added to it.**
`code.tests.loc.total` against `code.loc.total` is how much of the tree is
tests, and the `code.tests` arms are the only counters that include them.

A report of several crates is a table of leaves, one row per crate, with the
denominator beside every share.

### 3.2 What a comparison requires

The document is a pure function of the source tree under a fixed scanner, so
two figures are comparable only when the scanner and the flags match: the
ffimap commit, the toolchain, `--sys-crates` (which decides what
`ty.storing_raw_ptr` admits), `--seams` (which decides what the `seam` shares
and `casted_to.local_seam` can see) and any framework the crate is built on.
The `scanner` and `sys_crates` fields carry all of it, which is why they are in
the document rather than beside it
([analysis 1](analysis.md#1-determinism-and-what-it-rests-on)).

A counter added or a rule corrected moves figures too. The ones already known
to be incomparable across versions are named in
[analysis 12](analysis.md#12-what-the-analysis-cannot-see).

### 3.3 No target values

ffimap has none, and this is the place that says so. Absolute counts are not
comparable across crates of different size, and lower is not automatically
better: a wrapper over C must contain unsafe, and folding 600 small audited
blocks into 200 large ones improves the number while making the crate worse.
A reader who wants a rate divides the leaves it names.

Finding what is worth looking at is the opposite kind of work, and belongs to
a reviewer who reads the code, forms suspicions and defends them. `none` and
`no_seam_trait` name an absence, not a defect.

since folding small blocks into large ones moves one and not the other.
`code.unsafe_block.of_which.ffi_export` subtracts the gateways a port campaign
generated, and the `code.unsafe_call` arms say what the unsafe is for: `ffi`
is the boundary, `rust` is the standard library's constructors and the crate's
own helpers, `intrinsic` is `transmute` and its siblings.

**What the crate wrote, as opposed to what a macro did.** Subtract
`fn.total.of_which.macro` from `fn.total`, and
`ty.impl_trait.of_which.derived` from `ty.impl_trait`. A comparison of two
crates without those shares is partly a comparison of how much boilerplate
each spells.

**What the crate declares about the pointers it manages.**
`ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none` against `ty.storing_raw_ptr` is the types
that hold a pointer and say nothing about it. The other shares say what the
rest declared -- `impl_drop`, `impl_clone`, `ffibox` -- and `pub_field` is the
opposite of a declaration.

**Whether a convention is kept.** Under `--ffibox`,
`ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std` less `self_in_ref_accessor` and
`self_in_trait_impl` is the bare `&Foo` surface the convention says should be a
handle. `as.owned.std` and `as.by_val` against `as.owned.ffibox` say how much
of a cell's storage the crate holds itself rather than through ffibox's
owners. `ty.ffibox.wrapper.of_which.no_seam_trait` is the cells a generic
handle has to special-case, and `fn.sig.of_which.ffibox` whether the
vocabulary reaches the interface at all.

**What the trait impls do.** `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std`'s arms say which of
the crate's adopted traits act on what it wraps: `drop` and `clone` run its
lifecycle, `send` and `sync` are claims about threads, `ref_forming` can hand
out a reference to it. Under `--ffibox`, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.ffibox`'s
`layout` and `policy` say how much of the convention is the cells' layout and
how much their lifecycle.

**Whose shape the pointers in trait impls are.** `fn_sig_trait_impl` is read
through its `of_which` arms, never bare: one crate's are a convention's
lifecycle strategies, another's its own private helpers, a third's one local
conversion trait, and the bare figure is the same for all three.

**The test code, beside the library and never added to it.**
`code.tests.loc.total` against `code.loc.total` is how much of the tree is
tests, and the `code.tests` arms are the only counters that include them.

A report of several crates is a table of leaves, one row per crate, with the
denominator beside every share.

### 3.2 What a comparison requires

The document is a pure function of the source tree under a fixed scanner, so
two figures are comparable only when the scanner and the flags match: the
ffimap commit, the toolchain, `--sys-crates` (which decides what
`ty.storing_raw_ptr` admits), `--seams` (which decides what the `seam` shares
and `casted_to.local_seam` can see) and any framework the crate is built on.
The `scanner` and `sys_crates` fields carry all of it, which is why they are in
the document rather than beside it
([analysis 1](analysis.md#1-determinism-and-what-it-rests-on)).

A counter added or a rule corrected moves figures too. The ones already known
to be incomparable across versions are named in
[analysis 12](analysis.md#12-what-the-analysis-cannot-see).

### 3.3 No target values

ffimap has none, and this is the place that says so. Absolute counts are not
comparable across crates of different size, and lower is not automatically
better: a wrapper over C must contain unsafe, and folding 600 small audited
blocks into 200 large ones improves the number while making the crate worse.
A reader who wants a rate divides the leaves it names.

Finding what is worth looking at is the opposite kind of work, and belongs to
a reviewer who reads the code, forms suspicions and defends them. `none` and
`no_seam_trait` name an absence, not a defect.

#!/bin/bash
# baseline.sh <crate checkout> <package> <cov dir> <nightly> [cargo test args...]: as run.sh, for a
# comparison crate: its own C built by its build script, instrumented through CC/CFLAGS.
set -uo pipefail
trap 'echo "failed at line $LINENO" >&2' ERR
src=$1 pkg=$2 out=$3 nightly=$4; shift 4
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
tree=$out/tree
rm -rf "$out"; mkdir -p "$tree" "$out/prof"
(cd "$src" && tar -cf - --exclude=./target --exclude=./.git .) | (cd "$tree" && tar -xf -)
# a scratch copy inside another workspace's tree is its own workspace
grep -q '^\[workspace\]' "$tree/Cargo.toml" || printf '\n[workspace]\n' >> "$tree/Cargo.toml"
root=$(cd "$tree" && cargo metadata --no-deps --format-version 1 | python3 -c "import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin);p=[x for x in d['packages'] if x['name']=='$pkg'][0];print([t['src_path'] for t in p['targets'] if 'lib' in t['kind']][0])")
python3 "$(dirname "$0")/mark.py" "$(dirname "$root")" "$root"
cd "$(dirname "$root")/.."
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=$out/target CC=/usr/lib/llvm-23/bin/clang CFLAGS="-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping"
export RUSTFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage" RUSTDOCFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage -Z unstable-options --persist-doctests $out/doctests"
cargo "+$nightly" test -p "$pkg" "$@" --target $host --no-run --message-format=json 2>"$out/build.err" \
  | python3 -c 'import sys,json
for l in sys.stdin:
  try: d=json.loads(l)
  except: continue
  if d.get("reason")=="compiler-artifact" and d.get("executable") and d["target"]["kind"]!=["custom-build"] and d.get("profile",{}).get("test"): print(d["target"]["name"],d["target"]["kind"][0],d["executable"])' > "$out/bins.txt"
cat "$out/bins.txt"; tail -2 "$out/build.err"
while read -r name kind exe; do
  suite=$([ "$kind" = lib ] && echo lib || echo "$name")
  mkdir -p "$out/prof/$suite"; echo "== $suite"
  LLVM_PROFILE_FILE="$out/prof/$suite/%p-%m.profraw" "$exe" > "$out/$suite.log" 2>&1 || echo "rc=$? in $suite"
  grep 'test result' "$out/$suite.log"
  "$exe" --list 2>/dev/null | grep -c ': test$' > "$out/$suite.count"
done < "$out/bins.txt"
mkdir -p "$out/prof/doc"; echo "== doc"
LLVM_PROFILE_FILE="$out/prof/doc/%p-%m.profraw" cargo "+$nightly" test -p "$pkg" "$@" --target $host --doc > "$out/doc.log" 2>&1 || echo "rc=$? in doc"

"""mark.py <crate src dir> <crate root file>: put #[coverage(off)] on every test item."""
import re,sys,pathlib
src=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]); root=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[2])
ATTR=re.compile(r'^(\s*)#\[(test|cfg\((?:[^\]]*\btest\b[^\]]*)\))\]\s*$')
ITEM=re.compile(r'^\s*(pub(\([^)]*\))?\s+)?(const\s+)?(async\s+)?(unsafe\s+)?(extern\s+"C"\s+)?(mod|fn|impl)\b')
n=0
for f in src.rglob('*.rs'):
    L=f.read_text().split('\n'); out=[]; i=0
    while i<len(L):
        m=ATTR.match(L[i])
        if m:
            j=i+1
            while j<len(L) and (L[j].strip().startswith('#[') or L[j].strip().startswith('//')): j+=1
            prev=out[-1].strip() if out else ''
            if j<len(L) and ITEM.match(L[j]) and prev!='#[coverage(off)]':
                out.append(m.group(1)+'#[coverage(off)]'); n+=1
        out.append(L[i]); i+=1
    f.write_text('\n'.join(out))
r=root.read_text(); root.write_text('#![feature(coverage_attribute)]\n'+r)
print('marked',n)

"""report.py <cov dir> <name>=<dir>[:<dir>...][@<compilation dir>],... --c <C object>...

Merges each suite's profiles under <cov dir>/prof/, the four suites' union as TOTAL and every
suite's as ALL, and prints the TOTAL line of `llvm-cov report` for each named scope, with the C
objects and every test and doctest binary as objects for every suite. A scope's @<dir>
resolves the relative paths a C build recorded. MERGED=1 reuses the merged profiles, and ONLY=<suite> reports that one alone.

A scope written `<name>=@c`, such as `C=@c`, reads the C objects alone, with no source filter:
the archive holds only the link unit's TUs, whatever paths their build recorded. Any other
scope fails when a file it reports lies outside its dirs: llvm-cov falls back to every object
when its filters match no source, which would count the test binaries' std and Rust as C.

The C objects are those of the coverage variant's static archive, its `static` in build.json
(crustify/builds/coverage/crustify/libcrustify.a), which the test binaries link: each binary holds
only the TUs it reaches, so the archive, which llvm-cov reads member by member, gives every TU
its place in the denominator, one no test reaches at zero."""
import subprocess,sys,pathlib,json,glob,os
out0=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
nightly=os.environ.get("NIGHTLY") or next(l.split('"')[1] for l in open(out0/"tree"/"Cargo.toml") if l.startswith("nightly = "))
sysroot=subprocess.run(['rustc','+'+nightly,'--print','sysroot'],capture_output=True,text=True,check=True).stdout.strip()
B=sysroot+'/lib/rustlib/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bin/'
out=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]); scopes=dict(s.split('=',1) for s in sys.argv[2].split(','))
cobjs=sys.argv[sys.argv.index('--c')+1:]
bins=[l.split()[2] for l in (out/'bins.txt').read_text().splitlines()]
docs=[p for p in glob.glob(str(out/'doctests'/'**'/'rust_out'),recursive=True)]

rm -rf "$out"; mkdir -p "$tree" "$out/prof"
(cd "$src" && tar -cf - --exclude=./target --exclude=./.git .) | (cd "$tree" && tar -xf -)

grep -q '^\[workspace\]' "$tree/Cargo.toml" || printf '\n[workspace]\n' >> "$tree/Cargo.toml"

"""mark.py <crate src dir> <crate root file>: put #[coverage(off)] on every test item."""
import re,sys,pathlib
src=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]); root=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[2])
ATTR=re.compile(r'^(\s*)#\[(test|cfg\((?:[^\]]*\btest\b[^\]]*)\))\]\s*$')
ITEM=re.compile(r'^\s*(pub(\([^)]*\))?\s+)?(const\s+)?(async\s+)?(unsafe\s+)?(extern\s+"C"\s+)?(mod|fn|impl)\b')
n=0
for f in src.rglob('*.rs'):
    L=f.read_text().split('\n'); out=[]; i=0
    while i<len(L):
        m=ATTR.match(L[i])
        if m:
            j=i+1
            while j<len(L) and (L[j].strip().startswith('#[') or L[j].strip().startswith('//')): j+=1
            prev=out[-1].strip() if out else ''
            if j<len(L) and ITEM.match(L[j]) and prev!='#[coverage(off)]':
                out.append(m.group(1)+'#[coverage(off)]'); n+=1
        out.append(L[i]); i+=1
    f.write_text('\n'.join(out))
r=root.read_text(); root.write_text('#![feature(coverage_attribute)]\n'+r)
print('marked',n)

# Wave 3's write through a shared stream handle takes the stream's lock itself

Status: `open`. Filed by glibc-crustify `wave-2/batch-0/run-1` (2026-11-13), under the
default `repair` autonomy (`crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` gives no `evolution` answer): a correction
to a campaign artifact the planner owns, proposed.

## Signal

A plan that would ask a later batch for a binding its analysis cannot make sound
(`evolution` §2, "plan corrections"). Planner run 1 (`25b3fe2`) plans `fprintf` (wave 3) as
`fprintf(stream, "%s", message)` through `_IO_FILE`'s shared handle, on the ground that
"glibc locks every stream operation, which the binder confirms before a shared handle
writes". Wave 2's analysis does not confirm it for every stream:

- `vfprintf` (`c/stdio-common/vfprintf-internal.c:1540-1563`) locks with the
  `_IO_flockfile` macro, which `c/libio/libio.h:282` makes a no-op when the stream carries
  `_IO_USER_LOCK`. `__fsetlocking(fp, FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER)` sets that flag
  (`c/libio/__fsetlocking.c:31-32`). Native code, not Rust, sets it.
- `flockfile` (`c/stdio-common/flockfile.c`) takes the stream's lock (`_IO_lock_lock`) with
  no flag check, and the lock is recursive (`sysdeps/nptl/stdio-lock.h`: owner and count).
  So `fprintf` called inside `flockfile`/`funlockfile` is serialized whatever the stream's
  locking mode.

`File`'s `Sync` (`src/libc/libio/genops.rs`, wave 2) therefore rests on this rule: every
operation bound on `FileRef` holds the stream's lock, taken with `flockfile`, for the
whole of its access. A `Sync` that relied on the stream's locking mode would rest on data
the native code can change, which `binding`'s Safe boundary section forbids.

## Destination

A campaign artifact: `modules.json` and `schedule.json`, the planner's. `flockfile` and
`funlockfile` (`stdio-common/flockfile.c`, `stdio-common/funlockfile.c`, declared in
`libio/stdio.h`) join the plan ahead of wave 3, or in its batch, since wave 3's `fprintf`
binding needs them. They could also be bound privately inside `fprintf`'s module, as the
lock its one call takes, with no public API of their own.

## Change

Planner run 2 adds the two functions as items wave 3 reaches. The fixed-arity form stays
as planned: `flockfile(stream)`, `fprintf(stream, "%s", message)`, `funlockfile(stream)`,
with the count returned, or `errno`'s `io::Error` on a negative return.

## Validation

None yet. Wave 3's binder confirms it from `fprintf`'s analysis.

## Review

Not reviewed.

# ffibox: the shared seam's contract for a C object that locks itself

Status: `open`. Filed by glibc-crustify `wave-2/batch-0/run-1` (2026-11-13), under the
default `repair` autonomy: a documentation defect in ffibox that does not block the batch,
proposed.

## Signal

Two ffibox documents disagree (`evolution` §2, "skills that contradict each other", here a
tool's docs). `CCell::ref_from_ptr` (`src/traits.rs`, at `9c22a73`), which
`CRefSeam::from_ptr` forwards to, requires that "nothing may write it while the handle
lives except through a `Mut` derived from the same borrow". `docs/ownership.md`'s
shared-and-mutable table puts "routines that lock internally" on `FooRef`. The macro's own
`CCell` safety comment, "`$rf` has no write operation", says the same as the trait.

A C object that serializes its own state, such as glibc's `FILE`, whose every stdio
routine writes its buffer under the stream's recursive lock, cannot meet the trait's
wording. C writes such an object while a `FooRef` lives, on another thread too, and that
is exactly what the table allows. Wave 2 of glibc-crustify binds `FILE` opaque, as
`File`/`FileRef`, and states the contract for a stream on the type
(`src/libc/libio/genops.rs`): the stream stays open for `'a`, and whatever else writes it
does so under its lock, while the handle reads nothing without the lock. That is the
table's meaning, but it is not the trait's text.

## Destination

ffibox: `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s `# Safety` section, and the `CCell` safety comment
`define_ctype!` emits.

## Change

`ref_from_ptr`'s contract reads: "`ptr` must address a live, initialised `Self::C` (or be
null) that outlives `'a`, and nothing may write it while the handle lives except through a
`Mut` derived from the same borrow, or under a synchronization every operation reachable
through `Self::Ref` takes too (an object that locks itself, whose shared handle reads
nothing without its lock)." The macro's comment says that `$rf` has no write operation of
ffibox's.

A documentation change. No reproducer: no current consumer's soundness changes.

# Lessons of glibc-crustify

Rules that hold for this campaign alone, as `evolution`'s Lessons section describes. Every
run reads them before its first step.

## A batch's gates run with no build variant

**Rule.** libc is the system's, so `build.json` has no variants, and this tree has no
`cargo-variant` script. A batch runs its gates directly, each build in a target dir of its
own under `crustify/tmp/`:

- campaign mode: `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=<plain | asan-ubsan | tsan>` set on every
  `cargo` command that builds the tests, which then regenerate the bindings and check them
  against the committed ones;
- format: `cargo +<the workspace's nightly> fmt --all -- --check`, since `rustfmt.toml`
  uses nightly-only options;
- ASan: on that nightly, `--target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, with
  `RUSTFLAGS="-Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"`; TSan: the same with
  `-Zsanitizer=thread` and `-Zbuild-std`. They instrument the Rust alone, since the
  system's glibc is not instrumented, so TSan sees no race inside glibc;
- coverage: Rust only, measured as the parent's `crustify/scripts/coverage/baseline.sh`
  does, over a scratch copy without `c/`. Its `report.py` rejects the scope, since
  `llvm-cov` prints this tree's file names relative to `src/`, so the `TOTAL` line is read
  from `llvm-cov report` itself. The compile-fail suite fails in the marked copy, which
  only a nightly builds, and it covers nothing.

**Evidence.** wave-2/batch-0/run-1 (`libio/genops.c`) worked these out by hand.

**Scope.** Every batch until the tree gets a variant script.

### Wave 2: `FILE`, and the cells a system libc leaves empty

`File`, with its borrowed handles and no owner. Its row's `+LoC` counts the regenerated
raw bindings (153 lines) with the safe module and the tests. Its three `+UB safe tests` are
compile-fail cases of the one `compile_fail` test, so the suite's `#[test]` count in

Rust figure is line coverage over `src/`, measured on the pinned nightly with
`-C instrument-coverage`. `File`'s code is the expansion of ffibox's `define_ctype!`,

1	//! `libio/genops.c`: the generic stream operations, home of `FILE` (`struct _IO_FILE`).
2	//!
3	//! [`File`] is C's stream, bound opaque and borrowed: the routines that open, write and
4	//! close a stream are C's, and Rust holds a stream only through the [`FileRef`] that
5	//! whatever keeps it open lends.
6	
7	pub use ffi_import::{File, FileMut, FileRef};
8	
9	#[expect(unsafe_code, reason = "asserts the thread safety of glibc's streams")]
10	mod ffi_import {
11	    use ffibox::define_ctype;
12	
13	    use crate::libc::ffi;
14	
15	    define_ctype!(
16	        /// Wraps `st::_IO_FILE`
17	        ///
18	        /// Wraps `tdf::FILE`
19	        ///
20	        /// C's stream, `FILE`: a file, a buffer or a cookie behind glibc's stdio buffer,
21	        /// which C's stdio routines read, write and close. Opaque: the safe API reads and
22	        /// writes none of its fields.
23	        ///
24	        /// Borrowed only. C allocates every stream (`fopen`, `fdopen`, `tmpfile`,
25	        /// `open_memstream` and their kin, or the static storage of `stdin`, `stdout` and
26	        /// `stderr`) and releases it with `fclose`, and glibc keeps the address of every
27	        /// file-backed stream in its list of open streams, which `exit` flushes, from its
28	        /// opening to its close. So no `File` value exists in Rust, and no owner: a stream
29	        /// is reached through a [`FileRef`] borrowed from what keeps it open, the C caller
30	        /// that hands it for a call, or the program, for the standard streams.
31	        ///
32	        /// Shared. C writes a stream's buffer and state from every stdio call, under the
33	        /// stream's lock: a recursive lock of its own, which each stdio routine takes,
34	        /// unless the stream's locking is the caller's (`__fsetlocking` with
35	        /// `FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER`) or the routine is an `_unlocked` one, and which
36	        /// `flockfile` takes whatever the stream's locking. [`FileRef`] is `Send` and
37	        /// `Sync` on that lock: every operation bound on it holds the lock, taken with
38	        /// `flockfile`, for the whole of its access to the stream, and reads nothing of
39	        /// the stream without it. No producer yields a [`FileMut`]: nothing holds a stream
40	        /// exclusively.
41	        ///
42	        /// A stream C hands Rust is borrowed with `FileRef::from_ptr`, whose contract
43	        /// reads, for a stream: the pointer is NULL or an open stream that stays open for
44	        /// the handle's lifetime, `fclose` included, and whatever else writes it while the
45	        /// handle lives does so under its lock, as glibc's own stdio routines do.
46	        #[doc(alias = "_IO_FILE")]
47	        #[doc(alias = "FILE")]
48	        File,
49	        FileRef,
50	        FileMut,
51	        ffi::_IO_FILE
52	    );
53	
54	    // SAFETY: a stream is tied to no thread: glibc opens, writes and closes it from any
55	    // thread, its lock recording an owner only while a call holds it, and no `File` value
56	    // or owner exists in Rust (the field is private and this region builds none), so the
57	    // assertion covers only the exclusive handle, which reaches the stream as a
58	    // `FileRef` does, through its locked operations.
59	    unsafe impl Send for File {}
60	    // SAFETY: as for `Send for File`: the exclusive handle holds no lock and no state of
61	    // its own, only the pointer.
62	    unsafe impl Send for FileMut<'_> {}
63	    // SAFETY: nothing reachable through a shared handle touches the stream but under the
64	    // stream's lock: `FileRef` reads no field, and every operation a region adds on it
65	    // holds the lock, taken with `flockfile`, which locks whatever the stream's locking
66	    // mode, for the whole of its access, so that two threads' operations exclude each
67	    // other and C's locked stdio routines alike.
68	    unsafe impl Sync for File {}
69	    // SAFETY: as for `Sync for File`: copies of a shared handle reach the stream only
70	    // through its locked operations.
71	    unsafe impl Send for FileRef<'_> {}
72	    // SAFETY: as above.
73	    unsafe impl Sync for FileRef<'_> {}
74	    // SAFETY: `&FileMut` reaches the stream only through `as_ref`, a shared handle.
75	    unsafe impl Sync for FileMut<'_> {}

genops.c: wrap 1 item (wave-2/batch-0/run-1)

st::_IO_FILE
tdf::FILE

_IO_FILE and its typedef FILE are one opaque type, File, minted by
ffibox's define_ctype! with the borrowed handles FileRef and FileMut,
and no owner: C opens and closes every stream, and glibc keeps a
file-backed stream's address in its list of open streams. FileRef is
Send and Sync on the stream's recursive lock. Every operation bound on
it must hold that lock, taken with flockfile, since a stream set to
FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER makes fprintf's own locking a no-op. A later wave
borrows a stream C hands over, or stderr, through FileRef::from_ptr.

The raw bindings gain _IO_FILE and FILE (<stdio.h> joins wrapper.h).
Tests: three compile-fail cases (no File value, a FileRef bound to its
borrow, FileMut not copied) and three unit tests of the handles' seams,
run plain, under ASan, TSan and Miri.

Proposals filed: stream-lock-for-shared-writes (flockfile and
funlockfile for wave 3), ffibox-ref-contract-self-locking and
typedef-named-as-its-type. A lesson records how this tree runs its
gates with no build variant.

I bound `_IO_FILE` and its `FILE` typedef, tested them, and landed one commit, `915f5a4`, on `refs/heads/crustify/waves/wave-2`. One gate could not pass: the safe crate does not package, because its `ffibox` dependency is a Git dependency with no version. That was already true on the base. `libc-sys` packages and verifies on its own.

**What waves 3 and 4 get** (`src/libc/libio/genops.rs`)
- **One type, borrowed only:** `File`, opaque, with handles `FileRef<'a>` and `FileMut<'a>` from ffibox's `define_ctype!`, and no owner. C opens and closes every stream and glibc keeps each stream's address in its list of open streams, so no `File` value can be built in Rust. It carries both anchors (`st::_IO_FILE` and `tdf::FILE`) and both aliases.
- **Wave 4's `stderr`:** it gets its `'static` handle with `FileRef::from_ptr`.
- **Wave 3's `fprintf`:** it gets the stream pointer with `as_ptr().cast_mut()`.
- **Thread safety:** `FileRef` is `Send` and `Sync`, on the condition that every operation bound on it holds the stream's lock, taken with `flockfile`.
- **Raw bindings:** I added `_IO_FILE` and `FILE` to `allowlist.txt`, added `<stdio.h>` to `wrapper.h`, and regenerated them in campaign mode.

**The planner's lock assumption does not hold for every stream.** glibc's `fprintf` skips its own locking when a stream is set to `FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER`, and C code can set that at any time. Only `flockfile` always locks, and it is recursive. So wave 3 must call `flockfile`, then `fprintf(stream, "%s", text)`, then `funlockfile`. Neither function is scheduled, so I filed that as a plan correction.

**Tests**
- Three compile-fail cases: no `File` value can be built, a `FileRef` cannot outlive its borrow, and a `FileMut` cannot be copied.
- Three unit tests of the handles: null gives no handle, the handles keep the stream's address, and handles cross threads.
- No safe producer exists yet, so the safe-API UB tests come with wave 4's `stderr`.
- Rust line coverage stays at 100% (50/50); `File`'s code is ffibox's macro expansion, which counts at ffibox's source. glibc is not built, so there are no C coverage figures.

**Gates.** All of these ran on the batch's own base and passed:
- format, clippy with warnings denied, and rustdoc, all in campaign mode;
- the workspace's tests, plain;
- the module's tests under ASan, and my tests under TSan and Miri;
- the ffimap scan: no new raw pointers or public `unsafe fn`s, and no unsanctioned C borrows.

TSan cannot see inside glibc, which is not instrumented. I did not run BSan. Under the lock the wave branch was still at `e2f015e`, so the rebase was a no-op and the tree that landed is the one the gates tested. That is why I reran no gate: nothing new was combined with my change.

**Dashboard.** I filled the batch's rows in the Types tables, Coverage stats and the Rust LoC line, and left the usage cells to you. I also added a Notes entry on the cells a system libc leaves empty.

**Proposals and lessons** (all filed `open`; I changed no skill)
- `stream-lock-for-shared-writes`: schedule `flockfile` and `funlockfile` for wave 3. This is the planner's to apply.
- `ffibox-ref-contract-self-locking`: `from_ptr`'s contract says nothing may write the object while a shared handle lives. That rules out an object that locks itself, which ffibox's own ownership doc allows behind that handle.
- `typedef-named-as-its-type`: the conventions have no rule for a typedef whose Rust name is its struct's. I put both anchors on the one type.
- I created `crustify/LESSONS.md` with one lesson: the commands this tree uses to run its gates with no build variant.

My scratch builds are deleted (1.5 GB); only small logs and scripts remain in `crustify/tmp/`.
